evidence_summary: Fuzzboxes identifies the Sperrin Fuzz Box as made by David Sperrin in Southport. His son Simon Sperrin is cited for the production history, including assembly at the family home and fulfillment by David and Beryl Sperrin. The model was advertised repeatedly in the British music press during 1966.

Specialist Rosac research identifies Sierra Electronics as the pre-Rosac company that released the Nu-Fuzz around 1969. The evidence is strong for a distinct manufacturing company, but the chronology and exact corporate transition remain partly reconstructed rather than fully primary-source anchored.

Rosac operated its own manufacturing facility and made effects as well as amplifiers and PA equipment. Its dirt products include Nu-Fuzz, Nu-Wa-Fuzz, Distortion Blender and related effects. Fuzzboxes and Effects Database both document Rosac as the physical producer; Tone Machines provides additional production chronology and period advertising.

Effects Database catalogs the Rosac Nu-Wa-Fuzz as a Rosac product combining the Nu-Fuzz and wah functions. Tone Machines documents the Nu-Wa Fuzz in the Rosac production line and period advertising by November 1969.

Effects Database identifies the Rosac Distortion Blender as a Rosac product using a Nu-Fuzz-based design with a blend function. Tone Machines documents the Distortion Blender in the early Rosac product run and period advertising by November 1969.

Effects Database catalogs Rosac Nu-Wa as a Rosac effect. Rosac company history states the firm produced effects in its own warehouse/factory, supporting builder-level identification rather than a mere branded relationship.

Tone Machines identifies an early 1969 Don Wehr's Music City advertisement and proposes a Sierra/Rosac OEM relationship, but explicitly labels portions of the reconstruction as speculation. Keep as a candidate product/supplier relationship, not a verified builder record.

OzValveAmps documents a Fi-Sonic Fuzz-Blender MKIV and reports that company founder/operator Phil Dreoni confirmed the pictured pedal was one of his. Tone Machines identifies Fi-Sonic as an Australian amplifier brand that offered at least two fuzz effects during the 1960s, but notes the surviving evidence is sparse.

product_or_family: LPB-1 / Muff Fuzz / Big Muff Pi / Screaming Bird / Mole
evidence_summary: Electro-Harmonix was founded by Mike Matthews in New York in 1968. The early product run included LPB-1, Muff Fuzz and Big Muff Pi, with Screaming Bird Treble Booster and Mole Bass Booster also documented as early products. EHX and period-history sources provide direct builder-level attribution for the company's own effects.

Reverb and EHX historical material place the Axis fuzz in the early Electro-Harmonix period. It is a distinct EHX marketed product and should be enumerated under the builder rather than treated only as a Guild OEM relationship.

product_or_family: Guild Foxey Lady later EHX-built states
evidence_summary: The Guild Foxey Lady existed in multiple production states. Later versions were built by Electro-Harmonix, including a three-knob version that paralleled the Big Muff family. Keep the Guild label as a marketed identity and EHX as the physical builder for those period-specific states.

Fuzzboxes documents Rosac manufacture of Nu-Fuzz variants and notes OEM versions such as the Don Wehr Fuzz-Tone were rebranded Rosac Nu-Fuzz variants. The archive should enumerate the physical builder first, then record marketed-label variants separately when independently supported.
